Title: AKUH's 'Signs, Symptoms and Care' programme preventable renal stone disease among major causes of death in Pakistan
NewsSummary: "Renal stone disease continues to be a significant cause of morbidity and chronic kidney disease in Pakistan even though it is preventable," This was disclosed by prominent urologist Dr. Syed Raziuddin Biyabani at a public health awareness programme
NewsContent:
​"Renal stone disease continues to be a significant cause of morbidity and chronic kidney disease in Pakistan even though it is preventable," This was disclosed by prominent urologist Dr. Syed Raziuddin Biyabani at a public health awareness programme by Aga Khan University Hospital (AKUH) held at Indus Hotel, Hyderabad on Friday.

Dr Biyabani who is the Associate Professor and acting Head, Section of Urology, Department of Surgery at AKUH, Karachi was speaking at the 'Signs, Symptoms and Care' Programme of AKUH.

Addressing the audience, Dr Biyabani said that according to AKUH, the incidence of the disease varies from 2.4 per 100,000 population in the north to 200 cases per 100,000 cases in the south of the country. He added that the stones form in the presence of dehydration, hot climate, infection in the urinary tract and with excess calcium and oxalate and protein in the diet. Those patients with a family history of stone disease and those with certain rare metabolic diseases are also at risk of forming stones, he added.

Discussing the symptoms, he said that the patients with stone disease may suffer from pain, fever, blood in urine or at times with altered renal function.

Investigations are directed at looking for urinary tract infection, determine renal function and imaging studies, including ultrasound, x-rays or CT scan are required to look at the size, site and degree of obstruction of the stone. These also help to find out how best to treat the stone.

Currently, open surgery is only rarely required to treat the stones. Extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy is used to break the stones into small pieces which come out through the urinary passage. Endoscopy is used to treat stones in the ureter and urinary bladder. Larger stones in the kidney can be removed with Percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL), which involves approaching the stones through a small hole in the skin. This can be combined with lithotripsy to completely remove all stones.

"Once the kidney stones form, 50% patients have chances of recurrence in 5-10 years," Dr Biyabani informed the people. He said that stone recurrence can be prevented by treating and preventing urinary infection, increasing fluid intake, decreasing protein intake and moderation in diet. Alkalinization of urine with diet and in some cases medication can help prevent stone formation. Excess calcium and salt in the diet should be avoided while moderate amount of milk intake is allowed, he concluded.

Dr Nuzhat Faruqui, Instructor and Consultant Urologist spoke about the common urological problems in females. She pointed out that urinary problems in females are under reported and under treated because of the lack of availability of trained female urologists in the field, and also because of the reluctance of female patients to consult a male urologist. She also pointed out a widespread belief among women who think urinary problems are a necessary part of aging.

Dr Faruqui said that urinary incontinence is involuntary loss of urine that is severe enough to cause a social or hygienic problem. It is more common in elderly females. "The overall prevalence in Asia has been reported to be about 14.6% in females and 6.8% in males,' she told the audience.

Most of the urinary problems in females are not due to aging alone. With proper evaluation, most patients can be cured, treated or adequately managed with improvement in the quality of life, she stressed.

As part of its outreach programme and societal commitment to creating awareness of early diagnosis and timely treatment, AKUH has organised over 200 'Signs, Symptoms and Care' programmes in Karachi, Hyderabad and the UAE, benefiting more than 40,000 people. Similarly, Aga Khan University Hospital's Patient Welfare Programme offers financial assistance to those patients who are unable to afford the medical cost of treatment. In 2004, 74 per cent of all patients treated at AKUH were from low- to middle-income groups. Since the inception of this welfare programme in 1986, over Rs. 1.4 billion has been disbursed to more than 250,000 needy patients.
